unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify the types of personal protective equipment and what each item protects.
- Explain when to use gloves, gowns, masks, respirators, and eye protection.
- Apply the correct order for donning and doffing personal protective equipment.
- Describe proper disposal of used personal protective equipment and the role of hand hygiene.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Gloves are like a raincoat for your hands. They stop wet, germy things from touching your skin, just like a raincoat stops rain from getting you wet.

### Question 2

You only need gloves when your hands might touch something wet and germy, like a used blood tube. Clean jobs like answering the phone do not need gloves.

### Question 3

Gloves are like a paper plate: you use one, then throw it away and get a fresh one. You would not use the same plate for every meal all day.

### Question 4

Wash your hands before you put on gloves and again after you take them off, like washing before and after you handle messy paint.

### Question 5

Disposable gloves are like a tissue: once used, you throw them away. Washing a tissue does not make it clean enough to use again.

### Question 6

If someone is allergic to peanuts, you would not make their snack with peanut butter. The same idea: use a non-latex glove for a person allergic to latex.

### Question 7

Sterile gloves are like a brand-new, still-sealed bandage, while exam gloves are like a clean paper napkin. Both are clean, but only the sealed one is germ-free enough for special jobs.

### Question 8

You do not need a raincoat when it is sunny. In the same way, you do not need gloves for clean, dry skin, but you do need them for wet, messy, or germy jobs.

### Question 9

If your hands are covered in mud, you wash them before touching a clean white shirt. Gloves work the same way: take them off and clean your hands before touching clean things.

### Question 10

Take off a dirty sock by grabbing the outside, then use your clean bare hand to grab only the inside of the other sock. That way the dirt never touches your skin.

### Question 11

If your bike tire gets a hole, you do not keep riding; you fix it. A torn glove has a hole, so you swap it for a fresh one before you keep working.

### Question 12

A glove should fit like a good shoe: snug enough not to flop off, loose enough not to rip. The right size keeps you safe and lets your fingers work well.

### Question 13

The powder on some gloves is like dust that can carry allergy-triggering bits into the air. Gloves without powder keep those bits out of the air.

### Question 14

If your hands are covered in germs, keep them away from your eyes, nose, and mouth, because those are the doors germs use to get inside you.

### Question 15

When you carry a cup of liquid that might spill, you protect your hands. Gloves do that job when the liquid is a body fluid like urine.

### Question 16

Cleaning up a red, messy spill needs gloves for sure, and a splash guard for your clothes and eyes if it might splatter.

### Question 17

If a job involves blood, gloves are not a choice; they are a must, no matter how good you are at the job.

### Question 18

Gloves are like a fence between two yards: they keep germs from going either way, protecting both the patient and the helper.

### Question 19

Germs are so small you cannot see them, so a glove that looks clean can still be germy. Swapping gloves between patients stops those invisible germs from moving along.

### Question 20

If someone is badly allergic to cats, you keep cats away from them completely. For a latex allergy, you keep every latex item away and use the safe kind instead.

### Question 21

A gown is like a big apron that covers your clothes so splashes do not get on them, protecting your skin and outfit underneath.

### Question 22

You wear a gown when a job might splash, like painting or frying bacon. In the clinic, it is for jobs that might splash blood or body fluids.

### Question 23

Some aprons let water soak through, and some are like a raincoat that blocks it. For messy splashes, you want the raincoat kind.

### Question 24

A gown only works if it stays wrapped around you like a closed coat, so tie it at the top and the middle to keep it shut.

### Question 25

A gown is like a long coat that covers your body and arms, leaving your hands, head, and feet to be covered by other gear.

### Question 26

If your coat gets soaked with something messy, you do not keep wearing it all day; you change into a dry one.

### Question 27

A disposable gown is like a paper napkin: after you use it once, you throw it away instead of saving it for later.

### Question 28

Different gear covers different parts of you, like a coat covers your body while mittens cover your hands. You use them together for full coverage.

### Question 29

When a patient needs special contact care, staff wear a gown like a protective coat so germs do not get on their clothes.

### Question 30

A sterile gown is like a freshly sealed bandage with no germs, used for special clean procedures. An isolation gown is like a clean apron, good for splashes but not germ-free.

### Question 31

If a job might spray like a garden hose, you cover your clothes. An irrigation that can splash calls for a gown.

### Question 32

When taking off a messy apron, grab the clean inside and roll the messy part inward so the dirt is trapped inside, away from your hands.

### Question 33

A mask is like a screen on a window: it blocks big droplets from getting in or out while you breathe and talk.

### Question 34

If someone near you is coughing and sneezing, a mask helps block the tiny droplets they send into the air.

### Question 35

Some germs float in the air like dust. A special tight-fitting mask called a respirator filters those tiny floating germs out of the air you breathe.

### Question 36

A respirator only works if it seals tightly to your face like a mask that blocks dust. Before using one, you get checked to make sure it fits just right.

### Question 37

Every time you put on a tight mask, give it a quick check to make sure no air is leaking around the edges, like checking a lid is screwed on tight.

### Question 38

A mask has to cover your nose and your mouth at the same time, like a bandage covering the whole scrape.

### Question 39

A face shield is like the windshield of a car: it blocks splashes, but it does not clean the air you breathe. Only a respirator does that.

### Question 40

A wet paper towel does not work as well as a dry one. A wet mask is the same, so you switch to a dry one.

### Question 41

The front of a mask is like the outside of a trash bag: it may be dirty, so you keep your hands off it.

### Question 42

Take a mask off by the straps or loops, like taking off glasses by the arms, so you do not touch the dirty front.

### Question 43

Big droplets can be stopped by a regular mask, but tiny floating germs need a special tight-fitting respirator, so the gear changes with the germ.

### Question 44

A respirator is like a tight, well-sealed air filter, while a surgical mask is like a loose screen that blocks big droplets only.

### Question 45

If someone is coughing, you put on a mask before getting close, so their droplets do not land on your nose and mouth.

### Question 46

A surgical mask stops big droplets, like catching raindrops with an umbrella, but it cannot catch the tiniest dust floating in the air.

### Question 47

A respirator makes breathing a little harder, like breathing through a straw, so a check is done first to be sure it is safe for that person.

### Question 48

If a job needs a special safety mask and there is none, you do not go in anyway; you tell the person in charge so they can get you the right mask.

### Question 49

A disposable respirator is like a paper coffee filter: you use it once, then throw it away and get a fresh one, and you never share it.

### Question 50

When you are done with a used mask, throw it in the trash and wash your hands, like throwing away a used tissue.

### Question 51

Eye protection is like safety goggles for swimming or science class: goggles and face shields keep splashes out of your eyes.

### Question 52

You wear goggles when something might splash into your eyes, just like wearing goggles when it might rain juice while you are mixing.

### Question 53

Goggles are like swim goggles that cover just your eyes, while a face shield is like a clear visor that covers your whole face.

### Question 54

If a job might squirt or spray, you wear eye protection, like wearing goggles when you might get splashed while watering plants.

### Question 55

A face shield is like a clear window in front of your whole face, protecting your eyes, nose, and mouth all at once.

### Question 56

Shared goggles are like shared swim goggles: you clean them before the next person uses them so no one shares germs.

### Question 57

A face shield is like an umbrella that stops splashes but lets air flow around it. Germs floating in the air can still reach your nose and mouth.

### Question 58

Regular glasses are like a window with gaps around the edges, so splashes can sneak in from the sides. Goggles wrap around and seal like swim goggles.

### Question 59

Getting dressed in PPE is like getting ready for messy play: put on the coat first, then the face gear, and save the gloves for last so they cover the sleeves.

### Question 60

You put gloves on last so they tuck over your coat sleeves like a cuff, leaving no skin showing at your wrists.

### Question 61

Before you put on any gear, wash your hands first, just like washing your hands before you cook.

### Question 62

You put on the big coat first because everything else, like the gloves, goes over it, the same way you put on a shirt before a jacket.

### Question 63

The full order is like a recipe: wash hands, coat on, face mask, goggles, then gloves last. Follow the steps in order and nothing gets left open.

### Question 64

The coat goes on first, just like you put your shirt on before your jacket and gloves.

### Question 65

After your coat, you put on the face mask, and then the goggles go over it, like layering from the inside out.

### Question 66

Goggles go on after the mask and before the gloves, like the middle step in getting dressed.

### Question 67

When a patient needs both a coat-and-gloves rule and a mask rule, you do both in order: wash hands, coat, mask, then gloves.

### Question 68

You put goggles on after the mask so they sit on top neatly, like putting on a hat after your headband so nothing shifts out of place.

### Question 69

Taking off PPE is like unwrapping in the safe order: gloves off first, then goggles, then the coat, and the mask last, then wash your hands.

### Question 70

Your hands touch the most dirty things, so you take the gloves off first, like wiping your muddy shoes before walking inside.

### Question 71

After you take everything off, wash your hands last, like washing your hands after you finish a messy art project.

### Question 72

You keep your mask on until the very end, like keeping your helmet on until you finish taking off all your other gear.

### Question 73

Take off your messy gear right at the door before you leave, like taking off muddy boots at the door so you do not track dirt through the house.

### Question 74

For the second glove, slip a clean finger under the cuff and pull it off inside out, like peeling off a sock without touching the dirty bottom.

### Question 75

Take the coat off by the clean inside and roll the messy outside inward, like wrapping up a dirty shirt so the dirty part is trapped inside.

### Question 76

You take off the dirtiest thing first and keep the face mask on until last, like cleaning the muddiest boots first and taking off your face guard at the very end.

### Question 77

After the gloves come off, you take off the goggles, then the coat, and the mask stays on until last.

### Question 78

If your hands get damp or dirty in the middle of taking off gear, wash them right then before you touch your face or other gear.

### Question 79

Used gloves and masks go straight into the right trash bin, like throwing a used tissue away right away instead of holding onto it.

### Question 80

Things with blood on them go in a special red biohazard bin, not the regular trash, so no one accidentally touches the germs.

### Question 81

A bloody bandage goes in the special red bin, not the regular trash, so no one gets the germs on them by accident.

### Question 82

Wash your hands right away after taking off gloves, even if they look clean, because germs can hide where you cannot see them.

### Question 83

If your job needs safety gear, the boss provides it for free, like a kitchen giving you an apron and oven mitts.

### Question 84

Treat every patient's blood and fluids as if they could have germs, and put on the right gear for the job, just like wearing a seatbelt on every car ride.

### Question 85

If you need gloves and there are none, you do not touch the messy spill with bare hands; you tell the person in charge so they can get you the right gear first.
